Name: Ipsos
Methodology:
CAWI via Ipsos’ Access Panel Online; BEFORE COLLECTION:
- Sample: structure and representativeness
- Questionnaire: the questionnaire is written following a writing process including 12 mandatory standards. It is reread and validated by a senior level then sent to the client for final validation. The programming (or questionnaire script) is tested by at least 2 people then validated.
DURING COLLECTION:
- Sampling: Ipsos imposes very strict operating rules for its sampling bases in order to maximize the random character of the sample selection: random drawing, solicitation rate, participation rate, abandonment in progress, off target, etc.
- Field monitoring: The collection is monitored and controlled (penetration, interview duration, consistency of responses, monitoring of respondent behavior, participation rate, number offollow-ups, etc.).
DOWNSTREAM OF THE COLLECTION:
- The results are analyzed in accordance with statistical analysis methods (confidence interval versus sample size, significance tests). The first results are systematically checked versus the raw results from the collection. The consistency of the results is also checked (in particular the observed results versus the sources of comparison in our possession).
- In the case of sample weighting (marginal calibration method), this is checked by the processing teams (DP) and then validated by the study teams

Name: CIS
Methodology:
Information collection method: CATI
Sample: The reference population in CIS studies is provided by the National Institute of Statistics (INE) using data from the population register, which provides us with information on the population by the variables of sex, municipality, nationality and age. CIS subsequently transforms this data into the strata of sex, age ranges, size of municipality by autonomous community used in the surveys. The sample design, that is, the selection of people for the survey, is crucial, since it allows the data obtained to be used to describe and analyse the population from which it has been extracted, the universe. It must be taken into account that in a sample there is a margin of error, the magnitude of which is established in the technical sheet that accompanies each study and in which all the technical characteristics are specified.
Weighting: The sample is weighted by making a comparison between the composition of the sample and an adequate delineation of the universe. This delineation of the universe is provided by the National Institute of Statistics (INE). On this basis, a national weighting procedure is applied, using marginal and intercellular weightings. In this way, minimum variables such as sex, age, NUTS II region (basic regions defined by the nomenclature of territorial units for EUROSTAT statistics), educational level (using the classification of programmes, degrees and certifications in levels of training attained (CNED-A)) and size of the locality are introduced into the iterative procedure. This post-stratification weighting is also known as 'correction weighting' or 'total non-response weighting'. The CIS dataset always provides two types of weighting: a post-stratification weighting at national level (PESO) and a post-stratification weighting at autonomous community level (PESOCCAA). Depending on the sample size, in some studies a post-stratification weighting at province level (PESOPROVINCIA) is also provided. The average values ​​of the coefficients of the post-stratification variable at national level (PESO) are attached at the end of the technical sheets. For the estimation at the level of each autonomous community, the microdata file also includes the weighting for each of them (variable PESOCCAA).
